frontier.hypothesis: The $6 allocation for `disc` is reachable by REDUCING the reference count of the pseudo that must occupy $a2 rather than by lengthening its live range. s5 closed the priority axis assuming 5-6 refs (floor_log2 = 2, requiring live_length > 132); with 2-3 refs the floor_log2 factor halves and the requirement collapses to live_length > 22-33, which is entirely reachable in a 144-insn function.
frontier.mechanism: global.c allocno_compare sorts descending by floor_log2(n_refs)*n_refs/live_length (x10000). Allocno 117 is currently position 1 of 24 at 5 refs/6 insns = 16667, so nothing at all is allocated before it and only its own HARD-reg conflict set ({2,29}) can block a register - which is the real reason it takes $3. Dropping it below 116 (`dist_sq`, pri 909, allocated $5, ALREADY in 117's conflict set) blocks $5 with no new edge needed at all; 132 (`ud`, pri 7273, $4) then also precedes it, though an edge to 132 is still required for $4 - see the second frontier item.
frontier.next_probe: Look for a spelling in which target's six $a2 references (slots 90 def, 91 bgez, 92 sltiu, 97 copy source, 99 table index, 104 bltz) are carried by TWO pseudos instead of one - e.g. the fast-path table index taken from a separately-named value - so that the pseudo which must land in $a2 shows `Register N used 3 times across L insns` in .lreg. Read the .lreg refs/live_length line BEFORE judging by score: the s5/E3 priority model is validated and predictive, so the whole allocno order can be computed from one dump.

frontier.hypothesis: The `addu $a0,$a2,$zero` copy at target slot 97 is emitted by reload / asm-operand satisfaction, not by a C-level `u32 ud = disc;`. If so the correct source form is the no-`ud` one (s5 M1) and the attack surface moves from cse to reload.
frontier.mechanism: s6/E7 proves cse cannot leave both registers with consumers, yet target has `disc` read by the bltz at slot 104 and `ud` read by the island at 106 and the srlv at 118. Two registers with live consumers therefore cannot both be members of one cse quantity, so one of them must be created after cse - reload copies for an asm input operand, or a local-alloc split, are the candidates. s5's M1 build is the existing datapoint: allocno 132 vanished yet build_insns stayed at 144, so a copy instruction still reached the output from some later pass.
frontier.next_probe: Rebuild the s5 M1 form (`(&D_8008D118)[(u32)disc >> shift]`, keeping `ud` only as the asm input), dump, and locate the surviving `addu` copy across .greg / .jump2 / .dbr to NAME the pass that emits it. If it is reload, read reload1.c's handling of the `"r"(ud)` input operand and ask what would make reload pick a different register for it - that is the mechanism that produces target's two-register split.

frontier.hypothesis: Slot 88 (target `addu $v0,$zero,$zero` + `j .L8002D774` vs our `move $5,$0` + join jump) is decided in reorg.c, not in jump.c.
frontier.mechanism: s6/E11: jump2 merges all 9 return-0 blocks into 1 in every build measured; the 9 copies present in both the target and our 144-insn base build are re-materialised by reorg.c filling each `j <label>` delay slot with the instruction at the jump target and redirecting the jump past it. Whether the disc<0 arm gets its own re-materialised copy is therefore a delay-slot-filling decision.
frontier.next_probe: Dump the `if (disc < 0) return 0;` variant and read its .dbr function region against the base .dbr: find the `j` whose delay slot was NOT filled from the return-0 target (the 2 missing insns) and identify which fill_slots_from_thread / relax_delay_slots condition rejected it. Do NOT re-read .jump2 for this.
